newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank urges caution in stock market.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank urges caution in stock market.

text.p: Taiwan central bank deputy governor Hsu Chia-tung on Wednesday urged investors to exercise "extra caution" when investing in the rallying stock market.

Hsu rejected some analysts' view that current share prices -- the Taiwan index hit a six-year high at 8,655.82 on huge turnover on Wednesday -- should not be considered high compared with the market's all-time closing peak of 12,495.34 in 1990.
"The bubble economy was at its worst when the share prices reached above the 12,000-point level," Hsu told reporters.
"We cannot use that period as comparison. It was abnormal," Hsu said.
Hsu warned that Taiwan's stock market turnover rate and price-earnings ratio were far higher than other countries'.

The mass-circulation United Daily News said the Taiwan market's P/E ratio was 35, compared with 16.5 in the United States, 16.79 in Hong Kong and 14.9 in South Korea. Taiwan's turnover rate was at 47.39, far higher than the 4.9 rate in United States, 4.39 in Hong Kong and 9.18 in South Korea.
"Investors should be risk-conscious and be extra careful. What the central bank can do has already been done," Hsu said without elaboration.

Hsu hinted that the central bank was tempted to clamp down on the loose liquidity that many analysts believe has fuelled a 25 percent rise in Taiwan's share index in 1997 alone, but feared the likely economic fallout of such a squeeze.
"The entire society will pay a high price if the central bank chooses to take drastic measures to tighten its monetary policy," he said.

Throughout the 13-month rally, the central bank has stood by its "stable-to-loose" monetary policy because inflation has been low and the recovery slower than hoped for, though it revised the policy to "stable to loose, but not too loose".
The central bank issued T$5 billion in one-month negotiable certificates of deposit on Wednesday following a day of record turnover in Taiwan's red-hot stock market.
The central bank has consistently denied that its repeated issuance of the short-term instruments in recent weeks intended to take some of the fire from the sizzling stock market.
Analysts suspect otherwise, saying persistently loose liquidity has been a key factor driving a stock rally that has seen the index rise 80 percent since February 1996.
Some analysts say Taiwan stocks may have been overbought and that the rises do not truly reflect firms fundamental value.

Brokers said the market's bullish sentiment on Wednesday was helped by the government's hands-off attitude because -- until Hsu spoke out -- neither the central bank nor finance ministry had issued any caution over the sizzling turnover levels.
